question.problem: The sides (in meters) of a square are decreasing. At a particular moment, the rate of decrease of the area of the square is numerically equal to ten times the rate of decrease of the sides. What is the length of the sides of the square at that moment?
question.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=10\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ So, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 10\cdot \cancel{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}} & =2x\cdot \cancel{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}} \\ 10 & =2x \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, at that particular moment we have $x=5\text{ m}.$
